name: Galileo
intro: Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter. It found a hidden salty ocean under Europa’s ice, then was steered into Jupiter on 21 September 2003 and burned up. Nothing is left, so this model is a memorial in space above Jupiter’s clouds.
whyLeft: Its fuel was nearly gone. NASA steered it into Jupiter on purpose so it could never crash into Europa and carry Earth germs to a moon that might hold life.
repurpose: Nothing is left to salvage. But its greatest repair still inspires engineers: when its big antenna jammed, they rewrote its software from Earth and saved most of the science.

hotspots.title: The jammed umbrella
hotspots.text: This 4.8-meter antenna was meant to open like an umbrella, but in 1991 a few of its ribs stuck and it never opened. Engineers sent new software so a tiny backup antenna could squeeze the pictures home.

hotspots.title: Where the probe rode
hotspots.text: Galileo carried a probe here for nearly six years. It let go in July 1995, and the probe dove into Jupiter’s air five months later.

hotspots.title: The camera
hotspots.text: On the way to Jupiter, Galileo’s camera found the first moon of an asteroid: tiny Dactyl, circling the asteroid Ida.

photo.alt: A long cratered asteroid with a tiny round moon to its right.
photo.caption: Asteroid Ida and its tiny moon Dactyl (the dot at right), discovered in Galileo’s pictures in 1993.
photo.licenseEvidence: Commons page licence: “Public domain” (PD NASA); original source: http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/imgcat/html/object_page/gal_p44131.html (image link).

hotspots.title: The magnetometer boom
hotspots.text: Sensors on this long boom measured magnetic fields and found that Ganymede, Jupiter’s biggest moon, makes its own, the only moon known to do so.

hotspots.title: Nuclear power
hotspots.text: Two nuclear generators on long arms powered Galileo, so it could work far from the Sun for 14 years.

hotspots.title: Protecting Europa
hotspots.text: Galileo found strong signs of a salty ocean under Europa’s ice. That is exactly why NASA crashed Galileo into Jupiter instead of leaving it to drift into this moon one day.

photo.alt: Creamy white moon criss-crossed by reddish-brown cracks.
photo.caption: Europa in close to natural colour, from Galileo’s pictures. An ocean is thought to hide under this ice.
photo.licenseEvidence: Commons page licence: “Public domain” (PD NASA); original source: http://photojournal.jpl.nasa.gov/catalog/PIA19048 Also described here: http://www.jpl.nasa.

funFact: Space Shuttle Atlantis carried Galileo into space in 1989, and it flew past Venus once and Earth twice to pick up speed for Jupiter.
